Through the 2000s, callback nesting (Node 9) was simply how asynchronous code was written. jQuery shipped something called Deferred in 2011 — but its version was subtly wrong in ways that mattered: it did not properly assimilate returned promises, and it did not turn thrown errors into rejections, so the two most valuable properties were missing.

The community's response was to write a specification independent of any library. Promises/A+, published in 2012, defined precisely how .then() must behave — the state transitions, the assimilation rules, the requirement that handlers run asynchronously. Several libraries implemented it (Q, when.js, RSVP, and most influentially Bluebird). Because they shared a specification, promises from different libraries could be chained together — which is what "thenable" exists to support.

ES2015 standardised it, adopting Promises/A+ almost unchanged. That is unusual and worth noting: the committee ratified what the community had already converged on.

Two design decisions explain behaviour that otherwise looks arbitrary.

Promises are eager, not lazy. The work starts the moment the promise is created, not when you attach a handler. Eagerness was chosen because it matches how callbacks already worked — fetch() starts a request immediately. The cost is that you cannot "cancel" a promise, and creating one you never use still does the work. Cancellation was proposed for the standard and withdrawn, which is why AbortController exists as a separate mechanism.

Handlers always run asynchronously. Even if a promise is already settled, .then(fn) does not call fn immediately — it queues it. This was a deliberate fix for the "Zalgo" problem from Node 9: a function that is sometimes synchronous and sometimes asynchronous produces order-dependent bugs. The mechanism that implements this is the microtask queue, which Node 11 traces.

The mechanism — traced

The state machine

pending ──resolve──▶ fulfilled (holds a value)
   │
   └────reject────▶ rejected  (holds a reason)

Once settled, a promise can never change again. Calling resolve twice does nothing the second time; calling reject after resolve does nothing. This immutability is what makes it safe to hand a promise to ten different pieces of code — each gets exactly one outcome, exactly once.

That single property fixes the fourth breakage from Node 9: a callback might be invoked twice or never; a promise settles exactly once.

Creating one

function delay(ms) {
  return new Promise((resolve) => { setTimeout(resolve, ms); });
}

function readFilePromise(path) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    readFile(path, (err, data) => {
      err ? reject(err) : resolve(data);
    });
  });
}

That second one is promisification: the error-first callback convention translated into promise states. Node provides util.promisify to do this mechanically.

The executor runs immediately and synchronously at construction:

console.log("before");
const p = new Promise((resolve) => {
  console.log("inside executor");    // prints NOW, second
  resolve(42);
});
console.log("after");
// before, inside executor, after

And an error thrown inside the executor is automatically converted into a rejection — one of the properties jQuery's Deferred lacked.

Promise.resolve(v) produces a fulfilled promise, Promise.reject(e) a rejected one. Promise.resolve is idempotent — passing it a promise returns that same promise — which makes it useful for normalising a value that might or might not be async.

function getJobs() {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    fetch(url).then(r => r.json()).then(resolve).catch(reject);
  });
}

This is the explicit promise construction antipattern. fetch already returns a promise; wrapping it adds a layer that can only introduce bugs. The correct version is return fetch(url).then(r => r.json()). Only construct a promise when wrapping something genuinely not promise-based.

Consuming: then, catch, finally

fetchBoard(url)
  .then(jobs => console.log(jobs.length))
  .catch(err => console.error(err))
  .finally(() => stopSpinner());

.catch(fn) is exactly .then(undefined, fn). .finally(fn) runs on either outcome and passes the original value or reason through untouched.

The mechanically crucial fact: .then() returns a new promise. Not the same one. Its fate is determined by what the handler does:

  • Handler returns a plain value → the new promise fulfils with that value.
  • Handler returns a promise → the new promise waits for it and adopts its outcome. This is assimilation.
  • Handler throws → the new promise rejects with the thrown error.

Chaining, and why the pyramid flattens

readFile("config.json")
  .then(text => JSON.parse(text))
  .then(config => fetchBoard(config.url))     // returns a promise — chain waits
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(jobs => save(jobs))
  .then(() => console.log("done"))
  .catch(err => console.error("failed:", err));

Flat, not nested, and the reason is assimilation. Because the handler returned a promise, the next .then does not receive a promise object — it waits and receives the resolved value. That single rule converts nesting into sequence.

.then(config => {
  fetchBoard(config.url).then(r => ...);   // NOT returned — chain doesn't wait
})

Forgetting return inside a .then is one of the most common promise bugs. The outer chain sees undefined, moves on immediately, and the inner promise runs detached — meaning its errors escape the outer .catch entirely.

Now the error story. A rejection skips every .then handler until it reaches a rejection handler. So one .catch at the end covers failures from every step above it. That is try/catch behaviour restored for asynchronous code.

p.then(onOk).catch(onErr);   // catch covers p AND errors thrown inside onOk
p.then(onOk, onErr);         // onErr covers only p — not errors from onOk

And a .catch does not end a chain — it recovers it. Whatever the catch handler returns becomes a fulfilled value for whatever follows:

fetchBoard(url)
  .catch(() => [])             // on failure, substitute an empty array
  .then(jobs => render(jobs));  // runs either way

The combinators

Promise.all(iterable) — waits for every promise to fulfil, then fulfils with an array of results in input order regardless of completion order. If any rejects, all rejects immediately and the other results are lost (though the operations keep running — there is no cancellation).

const [user, settings, jobs] = await Promise.all([
  fetchUser(id), fetchSettings(id), fetchJobs(id)
]);

Promise.allSettled(iterable) — waits for every promise to settle and never rejects. Fulfils with {status: "fulfilled", value} or {status: "rejected", reason} per entry. Added in ES2020, later than the others, precisely because people kept needing it.

Promise.race(iterable) — settles as soon as the first promise settles, whether fulfilled or rejected. The canonical use is a timeout:

const result = await Promise.race([
  fetchBoard(url),
  new Promise((_, reject) =>
    setTimeout(() => reject(new TimeoutError()), 5000)
  ),
]);

The critical thing: race does not cancel the loser. The slow fetch keeps running; you have simply stopped waiting. For genuine cancellation you need AbortController.

Promise.any(iterable) — fulfils with the first fulfilment, ignoring rejections. Only if every promise rejects does it reject, with an AggregateError (Node 8) holding all the reasons.

The clean way to remember: all is "all must succeed," allSettled is "tell me about all of them," race is "first to finish, good or bad," any is "first to succeed."

Concurrency versus parallelism, made concrete

// Sequential: total = sum of all latencies
for (const url of urls) { await fetchBoard(url); }

// Concurrent: total = the slowest single latency
await Promise.all(urls.map(fetchBoard));

The second is dramatically faster and still runs on one thread. The requests overlap because the waiting happens in the runtime (Node 9), not in your JavaScript. That is concurrency, not parallelism.

A practical caveat: Promise.all over five thousand URLs starts five thousand requests at once, which will exhaust connections or trigger rate limits. Real code needs a concurrency limit — exactly the createLimiter you build in Stage 3, and what the library p-limit provides.

Unhandled rejections

Since Node 15, an unhandled rejection terminates the process by default — a deliberate change, on the reasoning that an unnoticed failure is worse than a crash. Browsers fire an unhandledrejection event and log loudly.

saveJobs(jobs);   // if this rejects, nothing handles it
const p = fetchBoard(url);
await delay(1000);
p.catch(handle);   // may already have been reported as unhandled

The rule: attach rejection handling at the moment you create or receive a promise, not later.

Two subtleties worth carrying

const p = Promise.resolve(1);
p.then(() => console.log("A"));
console.log("B");
// B, then A

The promise is already fulfilled, yet A still prints second. This is the anti-Zalgo guarantee, and Node 11 explains the queue that implements it.

Promises are not cancellable. Once started, the underlying work runs to completion. race with a timeout stops you waiting but not the operation. AbortController is the actual mechanism for stopping work.

In your project

Stage 3 of shortlist is a guided tour of this node. You begin having written the serial bug — eight sources awaited one at a time, three and a half seconds for work that should take four hundred milliseconds.

Then the combinator choice, which is the actual lesson. Promise.all is the obvious reach and is wrong here: one dead board rejects the whole batch and you lose the seven that worked. Promise.allSettled is right, because partial results are genuinely useful. Having chosen between them for a real reason is what makes the distinction stick.

Then Promise.race against a rejecting timer — because a board that hangs is worse than one that fails. That gives you three combinators with three distinct, non-academic motivations.

Stage 3 also pairs this node with Node 8: allSettled hands back {status, reason} per source, and the spec warns you not to flatten that too early, because the reason is what your error taxonomy needs to decide retry policy. And createLimiter is the concurrency cap described above — closures (Node 4) holding a queue, wrapping promise creation.

In qbank

Everything asynchronous in qbank is promise-based underneath, whether or not you see .then anywhere. A Drizzle query returns a promise. The Anthropic SDK returns a promise. When you read that code with async/await syntax, what you are reading is Node 11's sugar over exactly the objects traced here — and an await that throws is a rejected promise from this node, unwrapped.

The connection genuinely worth making concrete is BullMQ's retry behaviour. A job processor is an async function, meaning it returns a promise. BullMQ decides whether a job succeeded or failed by what that promise does: fulfil means done, reject means failed and eligible for retry with backoff. That is the whole contract. Which means — connecting back to Node 8 — a try/catch inside the processor that logs and continues converts a rejection into a fulfilment, and the job is silently marked successful and never retried.

The other place to look: if qbank calls the Anthropic API for several items, check whether those calls are sequential or use Promise.all. If sequential and independent, it is the exact bug Stage 3 opens with.

What an interviewer does with this

"What is a Promise?" Weak: "a way to handle async code." Strong: an object representing a value that is not available yet, which turns an eventual result into a first-class value you can store, return, and pass around. Then the three states and the fact that settling is permanent and happens exactly once. Then why it exists — the four things callbacks broke.
